title: Data Curation and Preprocessing for LLMs
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Data Curation and Preprocessing for LLMs ##### The benchmark score that was a lie A research group in Hyderabad trained a 3B model and reported 68.4% on MMLU — remarkable for that size, close to models four times larger. They wrote it up. A reviewer asked them to check for contamination. They ran a 13-gram overlap search between their training corpus and the MMLU test set. **4,100 test questions appeared verbatim in training data**, scraped from question-bank websites that had mirrored the benchmark. Their model had not learned reasoning; it had memorised the answers. Decontaminated and retrained, the score was 41.2%. Respectable for 3B, and honest. The uncomfortable part: **almost nobody checks.** Contamination is the default state of web-scraped data, because benchmarks live on the web and Common Crawl scrapes the web. Data curation is the least glamorous and highest-leverage part of LLM training. The Phi models made the point loudly — carefully filtered "textbook quality" data at 1.3B parameters beat models 25× larger on reasoning benchmarks. Day 6 said data is a ceiling; today is about how to raise it. ##### Where the data comes from | Source | Scale | Quality | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **Common Crawl** | 100T+ tokens raw | Very low raw | The base of almost everything | | **C4** | 156B | Medium | Filtered CC, heuristic rules | | **RefinedWeb** | 600B | Good | Aggressive filtering + dedup, CC only | | **FineWeb / FineWeb-Edu** | 15T / 1.3T | Good / High | Classifier-filtered, open | | **The Pile** | 300B | Mixed | 22 curated sources | | **The Stack v2** | 900B | Good | Permissively licensed code | | **Wikipedia** | 20B | High | Multilingual, small | | **Books** | 100B+ | High | Licensing is genuinely difficult | | **arXiv, PubMed** | 50B+ | High | Domain-specific | For Indian-language work: **AI4Bharat's Sangraha** (~250B tokens across 22 languages), **IndicCorp v2**, and the Indic subsets of CC-100 and OSCAR. All need the same filtering pipeline, and language identification on Indic scripts is its own problem — code-mixed Hinglish confuses most `langdetect` implementations. **The critical fact:** raw Common Crawl is roughly 95% garbage — boilerplate, navigation menus, SEO spam, gibberish, duplicated templates. The pipeline is what makes it usable. ##### The pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Raw dump
100 TB WARC"] --> B["Text extraction
trafilatura"] B --> C["Language ID
fastText"] C --> D["Heuristic filters
length, symbols, lines"] D --> E["Quality classifier
fastText / Edu score"] E --> F["Exact dedup
hash"] F --> G["Fuzzy dedup
MinHash LSH"] G --> H["Decontamination
n-gram vs benchmarks"] H --> I["PII scrubbing"] I --> J["Toxicity filter"] J --> K["Mixture weighting"] K --> L["Tokenize + shard"] M["~95% removed
at each major stage"] -.-> D ``` Every stage removes data. A typical funnel: 100 TB raw → 20 TB after extraction → 8 TB after heuristics → 3 TB after quality → 1.2 TB after dedup. ##### Heuristic filtering Cheap rules that catch most obvious garbage. Run these before anything expensive. ```python import re import math from collections import Counter BULLET_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*[\-\*\u2022\u25cf]") ELLIPSIS_RE = re.compile(r"\.{3,}|…") def heuristic_filter(text: str, lang: str = "en") -> tuple[bool, str]: """Gopher-style quality heuristics. Returns (keep, reason_if_dropped).""" words = text.split() n_words = len(words) if not (50 <= n_words <= 100_000): return False, "word_count" mean_word_len = sum(len(w) for w in words) / n_words if not (3 <= mean_word_len <= 10): return False, "mean_word_length" lines = text.split("\n") if lines: bullet_frac = sum(1 for l in lines if BULLET_RE.match(l)) / len(lines) if bullet_frac > 0.90: return False, "mostly_bullets" ellipsis_frac = sum(1 for l in lines if ELLIPSIS_RE.search(l)) / len(lines) if ellipsis_frac > 0.30: return False, "truncated_lines" # Stop-word presence: real prose contains function words if lang == "en": stops = {"the", "be", "to", "of", "and", "that", "have", "with"} if sum(1 for w in words if w.lower() in stops) < 2: return False, "no_stopwords" alpha_frac = sum(c.isalpha() or c.isspace() for c in text) / max(len(text), 1) if alpha_frac < 0.75: return False, "low_alpha" # Character entropy catches repeated-byte corruption (Day 5's spike) counts = Counter(text) n = len(text) entropy = -sum((c / n) * math.log2(c / n) for c in counts.values()) if entropy < 2.5: return False, "low_entropy" # Line-level repetition if len(lines) > 5 and len(set(lines)) / len(lines) < 0.6: return False, "repeated_lines" return True, "" ``` **Track drop reasons.** A histogram of why documents were rejected is the fastest way to spot a filter that is too aggressive — if 40% of your Hindi corpus dies on `no_stopwords`, your stop-word list is English-only. **Adapt thresholds per language.** `mean_word_len` between 3 and 10 is sensible for English and wrong for German (compounds) and for Devanagari (different tokenisation of the same content). ##### Quality classifiers Heuristics catch obvious garbage. Distinguishing a mediocre blog post from a good explainer needs a model. The standard approach: train a fast classifier on high-quality positives against random web negatives. ```python import fasttext # Positives: Wikipedia, textbooks, well-edited articles # Negatives: random Common Crawl # Format: "__label__high " one per line model = fasttext.train_supervised( input="quality_train.txt", epoch=5, lr=0.1, wordNgrams=2, dim=100, loss="softmax", thread=16, ) model.save_model("quality_clf.bin") def score_quality(text: str, model) -> float: labels, probs = model.predict(text.replace("\n", " ")[:5000], k=2) for label, p in zip(labels, probs): if label == "__label__high": return float(p) return 0.0 ``` **FineWeb-Edu** took this further, using Llama-3-70B to score 500K samples for educational value on a 0–5 scale, then distilling that into a small classifier applied to 15T tokens. The resulting 1.3T-token subset substantially outperformed the unfiltered version on reasoning benchmarks. **The trade-off nobody mentions:** aggressive quality filtering reduces diversity. Over-filtering toward "textbook-like" text removes conversational register, dialect, and informal usage — which then shows up as a model that cannot handle how people actually write. Keep some of the middle of the distribution. ##### Deduplication The highest-value stage. Lee et al. (2022) showed dedup improves quality, reduces memorisation of training data, and effectively increases your unique-token count. **Exact dedup** first, because it is nearly free: ```python import hashlib def exact_dedup(docs): seen, out = set(), [] for d in docs: normalised = " ".join(d.lower().split()) h = hashlib.sha256(normalised.encode()).digest() if h not in seen: seen.add(h) out.append(d) return out ``` **Fuzzy dedup** with MinHash + LSH catches near-duplicates — the same article with a different header, boilerplate variations, template pages. ```python from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH def shingles(text: str, n: int = 5): words = text.lower().split() return {" ".join(words[i:i + n]) for i in range(max(len(words) - n + 1, 1))} def minhash_dedup(docs, threshold=0.8, num_perm=128, ngram=5): """Remove documents with Jaccard similarity above threshold.""" lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=num_perm) keep, signatures = [], {} for i, doc in enumerate(docs): m = MinHash(num_perm=num_perm) for sh in shingles(doc, ngram): m.update(sh.encode("utf8")) if lsh.query(m): # a near-duplicate already exists continue lsh.insert(str(i), m) signatures[i] = m keep.append(doc) return keep, {"input": len(docs), "kept": len(keep), "removed_pct": round(100 * (1 - len(keep) / len(docs)), 1)} ``` **Parameters that matter:** `threshold=0.8` is standard for document-level dedup; `num_perm=128` balances accuracy against speed; 5-gram shingles are the convention. Lower the threshold and you start removing legitimately similar documents. **Scale.** MinHash on trillions of tokens needs distributed execution — Spark or Ray, with LSH banding to avoid the all-pairs comparison. Expect 20–40% of a web corpus to be near-duplicate. **Also deduplicate at the paragraph level.** Boilerplate — cookie notices, footers, navigation — repeats across documents that are not themselves duplicates. ##### Decontamination The Hyderabad failure, and the step almost everyone skips. ```python def build_benchmark_ngrams(benchmark_texts, n=13): """Collect n-grams from every benchmark you will evaluate on.""" grams = set() for text in benchmark_texts: words = text.lower().split() for i in range(max(len(words) - n + 1, 0)): grams.add(" ".join(words[i:i + n])) return grams def is_contaminated(doc: str, benchmark_ngrams: set, n=13, max_hits=1) -> bool: words = doc.lower().split() hits = 0 for i in range(max(len(words) - n + 1, 0)): if " ".join(words[i:i + n]) in benchmark_ngrams: hits += 1 if hits >= max_hits: return True return False def decontaminate(docs, benchmark_texts, n=13): grams = build_benchmark_ngrams(benchmark_texts, n) clean = [d for d in docs if not is_contaminated(d, grams, n)] return clean, {"removed": len(docs) - len(clean), "removed_pct": round(100 * (1 - len(clean) / len(docs)), 2)} ``` **13-gram overlap is the convention** (used by GPT-3 and most subsequent work). Shorter n-grams produce false positives on common phrases; longer ones miss paraphrased contamination. **Decontaminate against every benchmark you plan to report**, and say so in your write-up. A reported score without a decontamination statement should be treated with suspicion — including your own. ##### PII and safety Under India's DPDP Act 2023 and GDPR, personal data in training corpora is a genuine legal exposure, not just an ethical one. ```python import re PII_PATTERNS = { "email": re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]{2,}\b"), "phone_in": re.compile(r"\b(?:\+91[\-\s]?)?[6-9]\d{9}\b"), "pan": re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b"), "aadhaar": re.compile(r"\b\d{4}\s?\d{4}\s?\d{4}\b"), "ifsc": re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{4}0[A-Z0-9]{6}\b"), "credit": re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b"), "ipv4": re.compile(r"\b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b"), } def redact_pii(text: str) -> tuple[str, dict]: counts = {} for name, pattern in PII_PATTERNS.items(): text, n = pattern.subn(f"<{name.upper()}>", text) if n: counts[name] = n return text, counts ``` **Redact rather than drop.** Removing whole documents containing an email address would delete a large fraction of legitimate text; replacing the address with a placeholder preserves the content. Regex alone misses names and addresses. For higher recall, add an NER pass (spaCy or Presidio) — slower, so run it after the cheap filters have cut your volume. For **toxicity**, use a classifier rather than a keyword blocklist. Blocklists have severe false-positive problems on reclaimed terms, medical text, and non-English content, and they disproportionately remove text from marginalised communities — a documented harm, not a hypothetical one. ##### Data mixtures Composition matters as much as volume. You are choosing what the model becomes. ```python def build_mixture(sources: dict, total_tokens: float, max_epochs: float = 4.0): """sources: {name: {'available': tokens, 'weight': target_fraction}}""" total_weight = sum(s["weight"] for s in sources.values()) plan = {} for name, s in sources.items(): target = total_tokens * s["weight"] / total_weight epochs = target / s["available"] capped = min(epochs, max_epochs) plan[name] = { "target_B": round(target / 1e9, 1), "available_B": round(s["available"] / 1e9, 1), "epochs": round(epochs, 2), "actual_B": round(capped * s["available"] / 1e9, 1), "warning": "exceeds 4 epochs" if epochs > max_epochs else "", } return plan # A coding-focused mixture — the assignment coding_mix = { "code_github": {"available": 900e9, "weight": 0.45}, "code_docs": {"available": 40e9, "weight": 0.08}, "stackoverflow": {"available": 30e9, "weight": 0.07}, "web_filtered": {"available": 1300e9, "weight": 0.25}, "books": {"available": 100e9, "weight": 0.08}, "math_arxiv": {"available": 50e9, "weight": 0.07}, } for k, v in build_mixture(coding_mix, 500e9).items(): print(f"{k:16s} {v}") ``` **Principles for weighting:** - **Upweight high-quality, low-volume sources** — Wikipedia and textbooks are worth several epochs where web text is worth one. - **Code helps reasoning** even for non-code tasks; most general models include 5–15%. - **Keep 4 epochs as a hard cap** per Day 6's data-constrained scaling. - **Multilingual needs deliberate upweighting.** Natural web distribution gives you almost no Tamil; if you want Tamil capability you must oversample it, and the same applies to the tokenizer corpus from Day 4. - **Curriculum ordering** — higher-quality data toward the end of training — measurably helps, and is cheap to implement. ##### The datasheet Your mini project asks for one, and it is a genuine professional practice (Gebru et al., *Datasheets for Datasets*). Document: - **Sources**, with URLs, snapshot dates, and licences - **Filters applied**, with the drop rate for each - **Deduplication** method, threshold, and removal percentage - **Decontamination** targets and hit counts - **PII handling** and what was redacted - **Final mixture** with weights and epoch counts - **Known limitations** — language skew, temporal cutoff, domain gaps ```python import json from datetime import date def emit_datasheet(stats: dict, path="datasheet.json"): sheet = { "created": str(date.today()), "pipeline_version": "v3", "stages": stats, "final_tokens_B": stats["final"]["tokens"] / 1e9, "known_limitations": [ "English 78%, Hindi 9%, other Indic 6%, code 7%", "Web snapshot through 2026-03; no later events", "Decontaminated against MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval only", ], } with open(path, "w") as f: json.dump(sheet, f, indent=2) ``` ##### Common mistakes - **No decontamination**, producing benchmark scores that mean nothing. - **Skipping deduplication**, which costs quality and increases memorisation. - **English-only heuristics** applied to multilingual corpora. - **Keyword blocklists for toxicity**, with their documented false-positive harms. - **Over-filtering toward "clean" text**, losing register diversity. - **Dropping documents for PII** instead of redacting. - **No drop-reason tracking**, so you cannot debug an over-aggressive filter. - **Running expensive filters before cheap ones.** - **Repeating data past 4 epochs.** - **No datasheet**, making the corpus irreproducible and unauditable. - **Assuming natural web distribution** gives adequate coverage of any non-English language. ##### Hands-on: build the funnel Your practical task builds a cleaning pipeline with language detection, quality filtering, and MinHash dedup on a raw text dump. Instrument every stage with input and output counts and a drop-reason histogram. Print the funnel. Seeing 100,000 documents become 11,000 — and knowing exactly which filter removed which — is what turns data curation from a black box into an engineering process. The mini project produces a reproducible pipeline with a datasheet. Make it genuinely re-runnable: a config file with every threshold, a fixed seed, and a `make data` target. Then run it twice and diff the outputs to confirm determinism. The datasheet is the deliverable that separates this from a script — it is also the artefact a compliance reviewer would ask for. The assignment designs a data mixture for a coding model with justified weights. Use the `build_mixture` helper, then defend each weight in a sentence: why 45% code rather than 70%, why include math, why the web fraction is there at all. Check the epoch counts and flag anything above 4. A mixture table with reasoning attached is exactly the document a training lead would review before a run. ##### Key takeaways - **Data quality beats data volume** — filtered corpora at a fraction of the size consistently outperform raw web scrapes at scale. - **Decontaminate against every benchmark you report**, using 13-gram overlap; most published scores that skip this step are inflated. - **Deduplication is the highest-value stage**: exact hashing first, then MinHash LSH at 0.8 Jaccard, expecting to remove 20–40% of web data. - **Redact PII rather than dropping documents**, and use classifiers rather than blocklists for toxicity to avoid documented false-positive harms. - **The mixture is a design decision**: upweight scarce high-quality sources, include code for reasoning, cap repetition at 4 epochs, and deliberately oversample any language you actually want the model to speak.
practical_task_reference: Build a data-cleaning pipeline that performs language detection, quality filtering, and MinHash deduplication on a raw text dump.
mini_project_reference: Create a reproducible dataset preparation pipeline with a datasheet documenting sources, filters, and dedup statistics.
assignment_reference: Design a data mixture for a coding-focused model and justify domain weights with expected effects.
